name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,700

clue.text: Corrupt villain beginning to ebb into depression

indicators.note: a beginning is the opening part, so only the first letter of the following word is kept
going into something means ending up inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a cad is a dishonourable man, a scoundrel
first letter of ebb
a dent is a hollow pressed into a surface

explanation.surface: A wicked character whose plans begin to ebb away as he sinks into gloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' reads as low mood, but here it is a physical hollow, DENT, which holds CAD and E to make DE-CADE-NT.
explanation.definitionFit: Decadent describes moral decline and self-indulgence, so it is a fair synonym for corrupt as an adjective.

clue.text: Twice one's substituted for United? That's realistic

indicators.note: one thing substituted for another takes its place, so a letter is swapped out for a new one

blocks.note: twice as much is double
a, the indefinite article, means one
U is the standard abbreviation for United, as in football club names

explanation.surface: Someone weighing up a football result in which a single goal replaces the team, then deciding it is plausible.
explanation.walkthrough: In DOUBLE the U (United) is swapped for A (one), giving DOABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan that is doable can actually be achieved, which is what a realistic target or aim means.

clue.text: Get instruction to sheepdog

blocks.note: first meaning: to obtain or acquire something
second meaning: the shepherd's command sending the dog clockwise round the flock

explanation.walkthrough: Shepherds working sheepdogs use a fixed set of calls; 'come by' tells the dog to circle the sheep clockwise, the opposite of 'away'.
explanation.definitionFit: To come by something is to acquire or obtain it, often by chance, matching the verb get.

clue.text: Does taking time prevent...

indicators.note: something taking an item takes it in, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: does are female deer
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A question about whether pausing to think stops something, trailing into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Does' looks like the verb, but it is the plural of doe, female deer; DEER takes in T. The ellipsis links the surface to the next clue but plays no part in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To deter is to discourage someone from acting, which effectively stops or prevents the action happening.

clue.text: ...a lot of unnecessary drug paraphernalia?

indicators.note: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a word for not required, one letter longer than the entry

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: deterring the excess of equipment that goes with drug taking.
explanation.walkthrough: NEEDLESS loses its last S to give NEEDLES. The leading ellipsis ties the surface to 3 down only.
explanation.definitionFit: Hypodermic syringes and their points are the classic equipment of injecting drug users, so needles count as paraphernalia.

clue.text: Set off stuck in reverse, disheartened

indicators.note: going in reverse means travelling backwards, so the letters are read from the end
losing heart means losing the centre, so the middle letter is removed

blocks.note: stuck somewhere is trapped there

explanation.surface: A driver trying to set off but stuck in reverse gear, feeling dejected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In reverse' sounds like a gearbox fault, but it reverses TRAPPED to DEPPART, whose middle P is then dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off is to begin a journey by leaving, and depart means exactly to leave or go away.

clue.text: Imagine fringes of tunic getting altered - it's inexplicable

indicators.note: fringes are the edges of a fabric, so only the outermost letters are kept
altering something changes its form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
first and last letters of tunic

explanation.surface: Picture the hem of a garment being changed for no reason anyone can explain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Imagine' looks like the instruction to the solver, but it is the anagram fodder itself, with T and C from the edges of tunic.
explanation.definitionFit: Something enigmatic is mysterious and puzzling, hard to account for, so it is inexplicable.

clue.text: Observe commotion about woman's poetry, essentially

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so only the central letters are kept
about can mean around, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: ado is fuss or commotion
her is the woman's possessive pronoun
the middle two letters of poetry

explanation.surface: Someone watching a fuss break out over a woman's verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignore the comma: 'woman's poetry, essentially' is two pieces side by side, and the commotion word opens up to hold both, split after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To observe a rule or custom is to follow it faithfully, and to adhere to it means keeping to it the same way.

clue.text: Heavy metal - it could be symbolised by the introduction of Whitesnake

blocks.clueFragment: Heavy metal - it could be symbolised by the introduction of Whitesnake
blocks.note: surface reading: a rock music genre represented by the opening of a famous British hard-rock band

blocks.clueFragment: it could be symbolised by the introduction of Whitesnake
blocks.note: setter's reading: the first letter of the band's name is the chemical symbol of a very dense element

explanation.surface: A music critic saying the whole genre of heavy metal is summed up by the opening of a Whitesnake track.
explanation.walkthrough: Whitesnake is a British hard-rock band, which sells the music reading. Its introduction is the letter W, and W is the chemical symbol of this element.
explanation.definitionFit: Tungsten is one of the densest metallic elements, almost as dense as gold, so it is literally a heavy metal.

clue.text: Let in or on

definitions.note: shares 'Let' with the first meaning: let on

blocks.note: first meaning: allowed to enter
second meaning, borrowing the verb: let on, revealed or confessed

explanation.walkthrough: The two definitions share one verb: read 'Let in' and 'Let on', and each phrase has the same answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Admitted means both allowed entry to a place and confessed a truth, which is what letting on means.

clue.text: Verbally compare fungus with algae

indicators.note: done verbally means spoken rather than written, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: to liken is to compare

explanation.surface: A biologist discussing how a fungus measures up against algae.
explanation.walkthrough: The plant is often pronounced like 'liken', especially in Britain, though some say 'litchen'.
explanation.definitionFit: A lichen is a composite organism formed by a fungus living in partnership with algae, so the phrase describes it exactly.

clue.text: Sort to use 17, amongst others

blocks.note: first meaning: a kind or category
second meaning: to press keyboard keys, the space bar of 17 down among them

explanation.walkthrough: 17 down is the long key on a keyboard; using it along with the other keys is what you do when keying text.
explanation.definitionFit: A sort of thing is a kind or class of thing, and the noun type is used in exactly that sense.

clue.text: Amply recover after eruption of bile

indicators.note: an eruption throws material out in disorder, so the letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
a patient who rallies regains strength

explanation.surface: A patient making a full recovery after a bout of vomiting bile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' is positional: the recovery word comes after the jumbled bile, not in the order the clue reads.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something liberally means doing it generously and in large measure, the same as amply as an adverb.

clue.text: Seconds involving extremely rude customs

indicators.note: to involve is to include, so one piece is enclosed by the other
extremes are the far ends, so only the first and last letters are kept

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, a second, so seconds are mos
the end letters of rude

explanation.surface: A complaint about a moment of very bad manners at the border customs desk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Customs' suggests the border post, but it means social conventions. MO is informal British for a moment, as in 'half a mo'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mores are the established social conventions and norms of a community, which is the sense of customs here.

clue.text: Guns, and where one might find them

blocks.note: first meaning: weapons
second meaning: guns is slang for biceps, which are found on the upper limbs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Them' refers back to guns in the slang sense of bulging biceps, which are located on the limbs; the first meaning is weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Arms means firearms and weapons generally, and also the upper limbs, where flexed muscles called guns are shown off.

clue.text: Reason to restrict supply of booze

blocks.note: to ration is to limit how much is given out
ale is beer

explanation.surface: Someone giving a justification for cutting back how much drink is available.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply of booze' looks like one phrase, but it splits after 'supply'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rationale is the underlying set of reasons or logic behind a decision, so it is a reason in the noun sense.

clue.text: Authorise adjustment - it lengthens trousers

indicators.note: as a verb, to trouser is to pocket, so the run of letters is tucked away inside the words before it

blocks.note: the run of letters straddling the three words, ignoring the dash

explanation.surface: Giving the go-ahead for a tailor's alteration that makes a pair of trousers longer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' looks like the garment being altered, but it is a verb meaning pockets: the answer sits inside adjustmENT IT LEngthens.
explanation.definitionFit: To entitle someone is to give them a right or permission, so it means to authorise as a verb.

clue.text: Key location to get a drink that's out of this world

definitions.text: location to get a drink that's out of this world

blocks.note: first meaning: the long key on a keyboard

blocks.clueFragment: location to get a drink that's out of this world
blocks.note: second meaning, whimsical: a pub in outer space

explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of this world' sounds like praise for a fine drink, but it literally places the bar beyond Earth.
explanation.definitionFit: The space bar is a keyboard key, and a bar in outer space would be a place to drink beyond our planet.

clue.text: Boat to dock beside Irish islands

blocks.note: to dock a tail is to cut it short, to trim it
the Aran Islands lie off Galway in the west of Ireland

explanation.surface: A sailor bringing a boat into harbour next to some Irish islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dock' suggests mooring the boat, but it means cutting short.
explanation.definitionFit: A trimaran is a sailing vessel with a main hull and two outrigger hulls, so it is a type of boat.

clue.text: Rainbow iridescence originally seen in various types of mineral

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so the opening letters of the words are kept
various means in differing forms, so the letters take a new order
something seen in a place is inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: first letters of Rainbow and iridescence
taken as written

explanation.surface: A geologist noting a rainbow sheen on many kinds of mineral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Types of mineral' wants to be read together, but 'types' is anagram fodder and 'mineral' alone is the definition; the singular-looking answer is a mass noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Pyrites, iron sulphide, is a brassy crystalline mineral known as fool's gold, which can show an iridescent tarnish.

clue.text: Fat creator of Adrian M

blocks.note: Sue Townsend wrote the Adrian Mole diaries

explanation.surface: A cheeky jibe calling the author of a famous comic novel overweight.
explanation.walkthrough: Adrian Mole is the teenage diarist of Sue Townsend's British comic novels; cutting his surname to M signals cutting hers to T as well.
explanation.definitionFit: Suet is the hard white fat from around animal kidneys, used in British puddings and pastry.

clue.text: Rifle fire

blocks.note: first meaning: to plunder or ransack
second meaning: to dismiss from a job

explanation.walkthrough: Together the two words suggest shooting a gun, but both are verbs: one for looting, one for dismissing someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To sack a town is to plunder it as you would rifle through a drawer, and to sack a worker is to fire them.

clue.text: Spot with attendant exudation

blocks.note: to spot something is to see it
a page is a boy attendant, as at a wedding

explanation.surface: A pimple accompanied by oozing, in the most clinical language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' reads as a blemish but is the verb to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Exudation is fluid slowly oozing out through pores or cracks, which is what seepage describes.

clue.text: Price, say, a lunatic raised

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising something lifts it upward, so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: e.g. means for example, as 'say' does
taken as written
a lunatic is mad

explanation.surface: A complaint that a madman has put the price up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lunatic' reads as a noun but is used as the adjective MAD. 'What's the damage?' is informal British for asking the bill.
explanation.definitionFit: Damage is colloquial for the cost or price of something, as in asking what the damage is at the till.

clue.text: Some use elementary uprising for fights

indicators.note: some of something is only a part of it, so the letters lie inside a longer run
in a down clue, rising up means reading from the bottom upward

blocks.note: the run of letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A remark that basic rebellion leads to brawling.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from the end of 'use' into 'elementary' and are read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A melee is a confused hand-to-hand scuffle involving many people, so melees are fights.

clue.text: Minor role advanced by job centre

indicators.note: the centre is the middle point, so only the central letter is kept

blocks.note: to advance is to come forward
the middle letter of job

explanation.surface: An actor offered a small part through the employment office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Job centre' looks like the British state employment office, but splits as job's middle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A cameo is a brief appearance in a film or play, usually by a famous actor, so it is a small part.

clue.text: Still tense about election's initial turn out

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the letters run the other way
an initial is the first letter of a word, so only that letter is kept

blocks.note: even can mean still, as in 'even better'
taut means tight or tense
first letter of election

explanation.surface: Nervousness lingering over the first results of an election and its voter turnout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn out' poses as voter turnout but is the definition. 'Still' means even in the sense 'even more', and TAUT turns round after it.
explanation.definitionFit: To eventuate is to happen as a result or come about in the end, which is what turn out means.

clue.text: Bound to eat last bit of cracker that's stale

indicators.note: eating something takes it inside, so one piece swallows another
the last bit of a word is its final letter, which alone is kept

blocks.note: bound with rope is tied
the final letter of cracker

explanation.surface: Someone obliged to finish off a cracker that has gone soft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to' reads as 'obliged to', but Bound alone is the past participle TIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Tired describes something overused and lacking freshness, such as a stale joke or idea.

clue.text: Graduate managed to drink last drop of rum - he's often seen in the pub

definitions.text: he's often seen in the pub

indicators.note: drinking takes something inside, so one piece goes into another
the last drop is the final bit, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: BA is a Bachelor of Arts degree
to manage a business is to run it
the final letter of rum

explanation.surface: A graduate who finishes off the rum and is a familiar face in the local.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He's often seen in the pub' sounds like a dig at the graduate's drinking, but it is the definition: someone always there because he works there.
explanation.definitionFit: A barman serves drinks behind the counter, so he is a fixture whenever the pub is open.

clue.text: Maintaining locks in rich area that's been redeveloped

indicators.note: something redeveloped is rebuilt in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Keeping door locks in good order in a wealthy, newly regenerated neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locks' suggests security on doors, but means tresses of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Locks are strands or tresses of hair, so looking after them is the business of washing and styling hair.

clue.text: Setter's note rejected

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: a tenner is a ten-pound banknote

explanation.surface: The crossword compiler's message has been turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' reads as the compiler, but here it is something that makes milk set. The 's is 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Rennet is the enzyme preparation used to curdle milk in cheesemaking, so it sets milk and is literally a setter.

clue.text: Mail a newspaperman returned, at first showing indifference

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the letters are read in the opposite direction
at first points to the beginning, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: to mail a letter is to send it
taken as written
ED is short for editor
first letter of showing

explanation.surface: A journalist's post comes back, and at first nobody seems to care.
explanation.walkthrough: SEND, A and ED read backwards give DEADNES; the S from showing finishes it off.
explanation.definitionFit: Deadness is a lack of feeling or response, an emotional numbness that amounts to indifference.
